blocks.text: A hospital doctor writes 'patient had a bad reaction to a new tablet' on a safety report and sends it to the regulator. The regulator cannot tell which tablet, when it was started, what the reaction was, or what happened next. A report like this is worth nothing, while a complete one from a single alert clinician can change a medicine's label for millions of patients.

blocks.markdown: An **adverse drug reaction (ADR)** is a harmful and unintended response to a medicine at normal doses. A **suspected adverse reaction report** (in the UK, a Yellow Card) is how clinicians and patients tell the regulator about it. Reports are only useful if they contain enough detail for a safety scientist to understand the case and compare it with others.

blocks.title: Minimum criteria for a valid report
blocks.text: A report is considered valid when it has four elements: an identifiable patient (age, sex or initials suffice, not the full name), an identifiable reporter, at least one suspected medicine and at least one suspected adverse reaction. Proof that the drug caused the event is not required; suspicion is enough.

items: Patient details: age or date of birth, sex, weight if relevant, relevant medical history and allergies
Suspected drug: name (brand for biologics and vaccines), batch number where known, dose, route, indication, start and stop dates
Reaction: clear description, date of onset, how it was treated, outcome (recovered, ongoing, fatal) and whether serious
Other medicines taken, including over-the-counter and herbal products
Dechallenge and rechallenge: what happened when the drug was stopped or restarted
Reporter details so that the case can be followed up

rows: Reactions that may need intervention to prevent the outcomes above
blocks.caption: Criteria that make an adverse reaction serious (regulatory definition, not severity of symptoms).

blocks.title: Judging the quality of a report
blocks.prompt: A clinician reports: 'A 58-year-old woman developed jaundice 6 weeks after starting drug X (a new medicine marked with a black triangle). ALT 640 U/L. She was admitted and drug X stopped; jaundice resolved over 3 weeks. She also takes paracetamol occasionally.' Decide whether the report meets minimum criteria, whether it is serious and what useful details are missing.

steps.text: Minimum criteria: identifiable patient (58-year-old woman), reporter (the clinician), suspected drug (drug X) and reaction (jaundice with raised ALT): all four present.
Seriousness: the patient was admitted to hospital, so it is serious.

Useful additions: dose, exact start and stop dates, batch number, other medicines in addition to paracetamol, alcohol intake, viral hepatitis tests, and the outcome after stopping (positive dechallenge noted).
The black triangle means all suspected reactions to drug X should be reported, serious or not.

blocks.answer: The report is valid and serious; dose, dates, batch and exclusion of other causes would strengthen it.

blocks.markdown: **Prescriber responsibilities.** Clinicians are expected to report serious suspected reactions to established medicines, and all suspected reactions to newer medicines under additional monitoring (marked with an inverted black triangle) and to vaccines, and to report reactions in children and those from drug interactions or medication errors where harm occurred. Reporting is voluntary in many systems, but it is a professional duty in good practice. Reporters do not need to be sure of causality, should include as much detail as is known, and should tell the patient that a report has been made.

rows: Serious reaction to an established drug
Any suspected reaction to a black triangle drug
Well-known mild reaction to an old drug (for example mild nausea)
blocks.caption: What to report (principles, details vary by national scheme).
Reporting rate is not incidence, because only a small fraction of true events is ever reported.

blocks.title: Reporting rate versus true incidence
blocks.prompt: The regulator receives 15 reports of a reaction over a year in which 600 000 prescriptions of the drug were dispensed. Calculate the reporting rate per 100 000 prescriptions.

steps.text: This is a minimum estimate, since many cases go unreported.

blocks.answer: 2.5 reports per 100 000 prescriptions; true incidence is higher.

blocks.markdown: **From reports to action.** Reports are entered into a database, coded and reviewed. Clusters of similar serious cases, or events that are unusual for the drug, are flagged for medical review and may be compared with trial data and other sources. If the evidence supports a causal link, regulators can require an update to the product information (the summary of product characteristics and patient leaflet), issue a warning to healthcare professionals, restrict the indication or population, require additional monitoring or, in the worst cases, suspend or withdraw the licence. Rofecoxib, for example, was withdrawn worldwide in 2004 after evidence of cardiovascular risk.

blocks.title: A report need not be certain
blocks.text: Suspicion is enough. Complete, timely reports with dates, doses, outcomes and other medicines make the difference between a case that can be assessed and one that cannot.

points: A valid report needs an identifiable patient, reporter, suspected drug and reaction; dose, dates, batch, outcome and other medicines make it useful.
Prescribers should report serious suspected reactions, and all suspected reactions to drugs under additional monitoring and to vaccines, without needing proof of causality.
Reports are reviewed for patterns and can lead to label changes, warnings, restrictions or withdrawal.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT required for a report to meet the minimum criteria for a valid adverse reaction report?

options.text: Proof that the drug caused the reaction
An identifiable patient
A suspected medicine
A suspected reaction

questions.correctOptionText: Proof that the drug caused the reaction
questions.explanation: The four criteria are an identifiable patient, an identifiable reporter, a suspected drug and a suspected reaction. Causality is assessed later by safety scientists.

questions.stem: A clinician reports 'rash after antibiotic'. Which additional information would most improve the usefulness of the report?

options.text: Drug name, dose, start date, date of rash onset, other medicines and outcome
The patient's full home address and occupation
The clinician's opinion on whether the drug is generally safe
The cost of the drug to the hospital

questions.correctOptionText: Drug name, dose, start date, date of rash onset, other medicines and outcome

distractorRationale.a: Correct: these elements allow timing and causality assessment.
distractorRationale.b: Full identifiers are not needed and do not help assess causality.
distractorRationale.c: General opinion does not describe the case itself.
distractorRationale.d: Cost is not relevant to causality.

questions.explanation: Temporal relationship, dose, concomitant drugs and outcome allow assessment of whether the drug is a plausible cause.

questions.stem: A newly licensed drug carries an inverted black triangle. What does this mean for reporting?

options.text: All suspected reactions should be reported, whether serious or not
Only fatal reactions should be reported
No reports are needed
Only reports from pharmacists are accepted

questions.correctOptionText: All suspected reactions should be reported, whether serious or not

distractorRationale.b: Serious non-fatal reactions are also reported.

questions.explanation: The black triangle denotes additional monitoring because the safety profile is less established. Reporting all suspected reactions helps build the profile.

questions.stem: Which suspected reaction should a prescriber definitely report?

options.text: Anaphylaxis requiring hospital admission after an established antibiotic
Mild transient nausea after an old, familiar drug
A prescribing error that was intercepted before the dose was given
An expected temporary bruise at an injection site

questions.correctOptionText: Anaphylaxis requiring hospital admission after an established antibiotic

distractorRationale.b: This is a well-known minor effect.
distractorRationale.c: A near miss caused no reaction in the patient.

questions.explanation: Serious reactions, even to long-established medicines, should be reported. Minor, well-documented effects are not usually reported.

questions.stem: How do reports most directly lead to a change in a medicine's product information?

options.text: Review identifies a pattern or signal, evidence is assessed and the regulator requires an update
A single patient's complaint automatically changes the leaflet
Reports are ignored unless the drug is withdrawn
Only pharmaceutical companies can change labels

questions.correctOptionText: Review identifies a pattern or signal, evidence is assessed and the regulator requires an update

distractorRationale.b: One case alone seldom changes labelling without assessment.
distractorRationale.c: Many label changes arise without withdrawal.

questions.explanation: Reports are aggregated and medically reviewed, and a plausible causal link supported by evidence leads the regulator to require label changes or other actions.

questions.stem: A clinician must be certain that a drug caused an event before submitting an adverse reaction report.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Reporting is based on suspicion. Causality is assessed after pooling similar cases, so waiting for certainty delays detection of problems.

questions.stem: A regulator receives 36 reports of a reaction over a year in which 1 200 000 prescriptions were dispensed. Calculate the reporting rate per 100 000 prescriptions.
questions.explanation: The rate is 36 divided by 1 200 000, multiplied by 100 000, which is 3. This is a reporting rate, not an incidence.

questions.stem: Suppose only about 5% of true cases of a serious reaction are reported. If 36 reports are received, estimate the number of cases that actually occurred (assumption stated in the stem).
questions.explanation: If 5% are reported then reports equal 0.05 times the true cases, so the true number is 36 divided by 0.05, which is 720. This illustrates why each report matters.

questions.stem: A 44-year-old man develops angioedema 10 days after starting a new antihypertensive and is admitted overnight. Describe the information you would include in an adverse reaction report and explain why each item is useful.
markingGuide: Suspected drug name, brand or batch, dose, route, start and stop dates
Reaction description and onset date, timing relative to start
questions.explanation: Each item helps decide whether the drug is a plausible cause. Marking should reward completeness and a rationale for timing and concomitant drugs.

questions.stem: Explain how spontaneous reports of a suspected adverse reaction may lead to a change in the label of a medicine or to its withdrawal.
markingGuide: Reports are collected and coded in a database
Medical review of clusters or unusual serious events
Comparison with other data and assessment of causality
Regulatory decision to update the product information
Warnings to health professionals, restrictions or additional monitoring
Withdrawal or suspension if risk outweighs benefit
questions.explanation: A report is an early signal that must be evaluated. Marking should reward the chain from report to assessment to regulatory action.
